'''''Prunus serotina''''', commonly called '''black cherry''',<ref name="WiersemaLeón2016">''[https://books.google.com/books?id=AIrNBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA833 World Economic Plants: A Standard Reference, Second Edition]''. CRC Press; 19 April 2016. {{ISBN|978-1-4665-7681-0}}. p. 833–.</ref> '''wild black cherry''', '''rum cherry''',<ref name="NCCE">{{cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/all/prunus-serotina/|title=''Prunus serotina''|work=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|publisher=[[North Carolina State University]] and [[North Carolina A&T State University|North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University]]|access-date=October 17, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240713065231/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/prunus-serotina/ |archive-date=July 13, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> or '''mountain black cherry''',<ref>{{cite web|title="Prunus serotina"|work=Plant Database|publisher=[[Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center]] at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=prse2|access-date=October 15, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240826033502/https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=prse2|archive-date=August 26, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> is a New World [[deciduous]] tree or shrub in the rose family, [[Rosaceae]]. Despite its common names, it is not very closely related to commonly cultivated [[cherries]].

==Description==
''Prunus serotina'' is a medium-sized, fast-growing [[deciduous]] forest tree or shrub<ref name="NCCE" /> growing to a height of {{Convert|15-24|m|abbr=off}}. The [[leaves]] are {{Convert|5-13|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long, ovate-lanceolate in shape, with finely toothed margins. The fall leaf color is yellow to red. The flowers are small, white and 5-petalled, in racemes {{cvt|4|–|6|in|order=flip|cm|0}} long which contain several dozen flowers. The flowers give rise to reddish-black "berries" ([[drupes]]) fed on by birds,<ref name="NCCE"/> {{Convert|5-10|mm|frac=8}} in diameter.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|242417060|Prunus serotina|family=Rosaceae|first=Joseph R.|last=Rohrer}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a914|title=Prunus serotina - Plant Finder}}</ref>

For about its first decade the [[Bark (botany)|bark]] of a black cherry tree is thin, smooth, and banded, resembling a [[birch]]. A mature tree has very broken, dark gray to black bark. The leaves are long and shiny, resembling a [[sourwood]]'s. An almond-like odour is released when a young twig is scratched and held close to the nose, revealing minute amounts of [[cyanide]] compounds produced and stored by the plant as a defense mechanism against [[herbivore]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Black cherry (''Prunus serotina'') |url=https://www.extension.iastate.edu/forestry/iowa_trees/trees/black_cherry.html |website=ISU Forestry Extension |publisher=Iowa State University |access-date=2018-04-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cnr.vt.edu/DENDRO/dendrology/lab2.cfm?t1=1&t2=2&t3=128&t4=44&t5=35&t6=47&t7=48&t8=94&t9=99&t10=103&t11=111&t12=36&t13=66 |title=VT Forest Biology and Dendrology |publisher=Cnr.vt.edu |access-date=2012-10-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070913170941/http://www.cnr.vt.edu/dendro/dendrology/lab2.cfm?t1=1&t2=2&t3=128&t4=44&t5=35&t6=47&t7=48&t8=94&t9=99&t10=103&t11=111&t12=36&t13=66 |archive-date=2007-09-13}}</ref>

=== Biochemistry ===
Like [[apricot]]s and apples, the seeds of black cherries contain [[cyanogenic glycoside]]s (compounds that can be converted into [[cyanide]]), such as [[amygdalin]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Poulton JE |chapter=Localization and Catabolism of Cyanogenic Glycosides |year=1988 |title=Ciba Foundation Symposium 140 - Cyanide Compounds in Biology |series=Novartis Foundation Symposia |volume=140 |pages=67–91 |doi=10.1002/9780470513712.ch6 |isbn=978-0-470-51371-2 |pmid=3073063}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Swain E, Poulton JE |date=October 1994 |title=Utilization of Amygdalin during Seedling Development of Prunus serotina |journal=Plant Physiology |volume=106 |issue=2 |pages=437–445 |doi=10.1104/pp.106.2.437 |pmc=159548 |pmid=12232341}}</ref> These compounds release [[hydrogen cyanide]] when the seed is ground or minced, which releases enzymes that break down the compounds.{{clarify|Into what?|date=June 2020}} These enzymes include [[amygdalin beta-glucosidase]], [[prunasin beta-glucosidase]] and [[mandelonitrile lyase]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Yemm RS, Poulton JE |date=June 1986 |title=Isolation and characterization of multiple forms of mandelonitrile lyase from mature black cherry (Prunus serotina Ehrh.) seeds |journal=Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics |volume=247 |issue=2 |pages=440–5 |doi=10.1016/0003-9861(86)90604-1 |pmid=3717954}}</ref> In contrast, although the flesh of black cherries also contains these glycosides, it does not contain the enzymes needed to convert them to cyanide, so the flesh is safe to eat.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Swain E, Li CP, Poulton JE |date=April 1992 |title=Development of the Potential for Cyanogenesis in Maturing Black Cherry (Prunus serotina Ehrh.) Fruits |journal=Plant Physiology |volume=98 |issue=4 |pages=1423–1428 |doi=10.1104/pp.98.4.1423 |pmc=1080367 |pmid=16668810}}</ref>

The foliage, particularly when wilted, also contains cyanogenic glycosides, which convert to hydrogen cyanide if eaten by animals.<ref name="mp">{{Missouri Plants|color=White|leaf=alt|genus=Prunus|species=serotina}}</ref> Farmers are recommended to remove any trees that fall in a field containing livestock, because the wilted leaves could poison the animals. Removal is not always practical, though, because these trees often grow in very large numbers on farms, taking advantage of the light brought about by mowing and grazing. Entire [[fencerow]]s can be lined with this poisonous tree, making it difficult to monitor all the branches falling into the grazing area. Black cherry is a leading cause of livestock illness,{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} and grazing animals' access to it should be limited.

=== Similar species ===
Black cherry is closely related to the chokecherry (''[[Prunus virginiana]]''), which tends to be shorter (a shrub or small tree) and has smaller, less glossy leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Deane |first=Green |date=2011-09-27 |title=Black Cherry: Chokecherry’s Better Cousin |url=https://www.eattheweeds.com/black-cherry-chokecherrys-better-cousin/ |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=Eat The Weeds and other things, too |language=en-US}}</ref>

En: Manual de Plantas de Costa Rica. Vol. VII. B.E. Hammel, M.H. Grayum, C. Herrera & N. Zamora (eds.). == Ecology ==

[[File:Eriophyes cerasicrumena. Shenandoah.jpg|thumb|Galls made by the mite ''[[Eriophyes cerasicrumena]]'']]
[[File:Black knot on black cherry0.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Black knot]] infection]]''Prunus serotina'' is a [[pioneer species]]. In the [[Midwest]], it is seen growing mostly in old fields with other sunlight-loving species, such as [[black walnut]], [[black locust]], and [[Celtis|hackberry]]. Gleason and Cronquist (1991) describe ''P. serotina'' as "[f]ormerly a forest tree, now abundant as a weed-tree of roadsides, waste land, and forest-margins".<ref>Gleason, Henry A. and Arthur Cronquist. 1991. "Manual of Vascular Plants of Northeastern United States and Adjacent Canada, Second Edition." The New York Botanical Garden. Bronx, New York.</ref> It is a moderately long-lived tree, with recorded ages reaching 258 years. It is prone to storm damage, with branches breaking easily; any decay resulting from it however, progresses slowly.

Some seeds may remain in the [[Soil seed bank|soil bank]] and not germinate for as long as three years. All ''Prunus'' species have hard seeds that benefit from [[Scarification (botany)|scarification]] to germinate (which in nature is produced by passing through an animal's digestive tract).{{cn|date=December 2023}} The tree is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] and can tolerate poor soils and oceanic salt sprays.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sargent |first=Charles Sprague |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iCE-AQAAMAAJ&dq=%22maine%22+%22tree%22+%22salt+spray%22&pg=RA1-PA5 |title=Some Additional Notes Upon Trees and Tree Planting in Massachusetts |date=1876 |publisher=Rand, Avery & Company |language=en}}</ref>

The species hosts the caterpillars of more than 450 species of butterflies and moths, including those of the [[Papilio glaucus|eastern tiger swallowtail]], [[Celastrina serotina|cherry gall azure]], [[Viceroy (butterfly)|viceroy]], and [[Limenitis arthemis|red-spotted purple/white admiral]] butterflies and the [[Hyalophora cecropia|cecropia]], [[Callosamia promethea|promethea]], [[Antheraea polyphemus|polyphemus]], [[Paonias myops|small-eyed sphinx]], [[Sphinx drupiferarum|wild cherry sphinx]], [[Halysidota tessellaris|banded tussock]], [[Apatelodes torrefacta|spotted apatelodes]], and band-edged prominent moths.<ref>Multiple sources:

=== Pests and diseases ===
''[[Hyphantria cunea]]'' can inhibit the impact of cyanide within the plants' leaves due to its alkaline stomach acid.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fitzgerald |first1=T. D. |title=Larvae of the fall webworm, Hyphantria cunea, inhibit cyanogenesis in Prunus serotina |journal=Journal of Experimental Biology |date=1 March 2008 |volume=211 |issue=5 |pages=671–677 |doi=10.1242/jeb.013664 |pmid=18281329 |bibcode=2008JExpB.211..671F |url=https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/5/671/18112/Larvae-of-the-fall-webworm-Hyphantria-cunea}}</ref> The [[eastern tent caterpillar]] defoliates entire groves some springs.

== Cultivation and uses ==
''Prunus serotina'' subsp. ''capuli'' was cultivated in Central and South America well before European contact.<ref name="Capulin">{{cite book |last=Morton |first=Julia |chapter-url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/capulin.html |chapter=Capulin|title=Fruits of warm climates |year=1987 |location=Miami, FL |pages=108–109 |author-link=Julia Morton |publisher=Florida Flair Books|isbn= 0-9610184-1-0|access-date=15 October 2013}}</ref>

Known as capolcuahuitl in [[Nahuatl]] (the source of the ''capuli'' epithet), it was an important food in pre-Columbian Mexico. Edible raw, the fruit is also made into jelly, and the juice can be used as a drink mixer, hence the common name 'rum cherry'.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Angier|first=Bradford|url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetoedib00angi/page/190/mode/2up|title=Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants|publisher=Stackpole Books|year=1974|isbn=0-8117-0616-8|location=Harrisburg, PA|page=190|oclc=799792|author-link=Bradford Angier}}</ref>
[[File:Quartersawn Cherry Lumber.jpg|alt=American Black Cherry quarter-sawn rift quarter|thumb|Quartersawn Cherry Lumber has vertical grainlines that match well with plywoods and veneers.]]
''Prunus serotina'' [[timber]] is valuable, perhaps the premier [[cabinet (furniture)|cabinetry]] timber of the U.S., traded as "cherry". High quality cherry timber is known for its strong orange hues, tight grain and high price. Low-quality wood, as well as the sap wood, can be more tan. Its density when dried is around {{cvt|560|kg/m3|lb/cuft|lk=out}}.<ref>[https://www.wood-database.com/black-cherry/ Wood Database: Black Cherry]. Accessed September 16, 2024.</ref>

''Prunus serotina'' was widely introduced into Western and Central Europe as an [[ornamental tree]]<ref name="FoNWE">{{cite web |author1=C. Stace |name-list-style=amp |editor2=I. de Kort |title=''Prunus serotina'' (Cherry, Rum) |url=http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2722 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071206130454/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2722 |archive-date=2007-12-06 |website=Flora of NW Europe |editor1=R. van der Meijden}}</ref> in the mid-20th century,<ref>Starfinger U. 1997.
